headline: Nvidia tells partners to pause server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia after new US rule tightens China chip access

facts.text: Nvidia has told manufacturing partners, including Dell and Super Micro, to pause server shipments to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, according to the Wall Street Journal.
The pause has no set end date and is in place while Nvidia assesses whether its regional partners are meeting U.S. export requirements.
Chinese companies had been tapping Nvidia chips remotely from data centers in the region, a loophole the US Commerce Department closed earlier this month.
The Wall Street Journal reports that Washington recently closed a remote-access loophole that helped Chinese companies tap into computing power in the region.
The New York Times reports that the shipping halt hit four countries and follows a new US rule that would require licenses for companies in those countries to buy advanced AI chips.
The Institute for Progress, a think tank, estimates remote data centers like these supply about 24% of China's AI computing power.
The US Commerce Department reportedly closed the loophole grudgingly.

context: Nvidia designs the advanced AI chips used to build servers in data centers, and its manufacturing partners such as Dell and Super Micro assemble those servers for customers. Export controls are US rules that restrict which foreign buyers and countries can receive advanced chips. Remote access means a company can use chips physically located in another country over the internet without owning them.
why_it_matters: The pause affects server makers and customers in Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia, and the new US rule tightens how advanced chips can reach China through the region. The sources say the closure of the remote-access loophole is significant because remote data centers in the region reportedly supply a large share of China's AI computing power.
open_questions: How long the shipment pause will last is not stated.
Whether Nvidia's regional partners are found to be meeting US export requirements is not yet known.
The exact terms of the new US licensing rule are not detailed in the sources.

headline: US approves Musk's plan for a million Starmind data-center satellites

facts.text: US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space.

Under the FCC licence, deployment must begin no later than November 2033, with 10% deployed by November 2035 and 50% by November 2038.
SpaceX has said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.
It is unclear whether a million satellites will indeed be launched or whether SpaceX sought approval for a higher number than it will use.

context: SpaceX is Elon Musk's rocket and satellite company, which operates the Starlink internet network of more than 10,000 satellites in low-Earth orbit. why_it_matters: The approval allows SpaceX to deploy a very large satellite constellation for AI computing, which astronomers say could make the night sky much harder to observe. headline: Hochul vetoes New York AI safety bill; California governor urged to act on AI safety bills

Newsom said he would welcome a special session but needed legislative partners willing to act, and had not yet called one.
Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra has endorsed expanded incident reporting and shutdown authority and said he would work quickly with lawmakers to enact both.
Newsom said waiting for Becerra to take office could delay the legislation by five or six months.
The recommendations came from an executive order Newsom issued Sept. 18, and an 85-page report from the Government Operations Agency was issued Nov. 16.

headline: New US chip export rule halts Nvidia server shipments to Southeast Asia and slows data-center investment

facts.text: Nvidia has reportedly ordered its manufacturing partners to stop shipping servers to Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand and Indonesia.
The halt follows an interim final rule issued by the US Department of Commerce earlier this month.
The Financial Times reports that Dell and Supermicro told customers in affected countries that Nvidia stopped server orders being shipped.
It is unclear whether the shipment halt is temporary, according to the FT report.
The Bureau of Industry & Security issued the new rule on November 16, requiring licenses to export advanced semiconductors to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil.
The rule describes these countries as presenting a higher-than-normal risk of diversion.
The rule also restricts remote access to advanced AI chips and servers so restrictions cannot be circumvented through data centers in third countries.
Citing Nvidia company accounts, the FT noted Nvidia booked $104 billion in 2025 revenue through its Singapore subsidiary, a 72 percent increase over a 12-month period.
The rule was issued in the fallout from Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's admission that he had an affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

Alice Huang, an executive for Singapore-based Megaspeed, is under investigation for smuggling Nvidia GPUs into China; the US added Megaspeed and its Thai and Malaysian subsidiaries to the Entity List.
Jensen Huang resigned on November 12 but was reinstated by the Nvidia board eleven days later, after pressure from President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance.

context: Nvidia designs the advanced graphics processors (GPUs) used to train and run AI models, and its partners such as Dell and Supermicro assemble them into servers. US export controls limit which countries can receive these chips, to stop them reaching restricted destinations such as China. Data centers are large facilities that house these servers and rent out computing power.
why_it_matters: The rule could disrupt server supply and AI data-center projects across Southeast Asia, affecting Nvidia's partners and their customers. Nvidia's Singapore subsidiary accounts for a large share of its revenue, so the halt is significant for the company's business.
open_questions: Whether the shipment halt to the four countries is temporary.
How long the licensing requirements will apply and how they will be enforced.
Whether the rule's remote-access restrictions will change how data centers in third countries operate.

headline: Massachusetts will require new data centers to use clean energy
Governments extend nuclear plant lifetimes as new builds suffer delays and cost rises

facts.text: The Financial Times reports that governments around the world are increasingly looking at extending the life of existing power stations.
The Financial Times reports that the extensions aim to meet rising demand for electricity.
The Financial Times reports that the extensions raise the prospect of 100-year-old reactors.

context: Nuclear power stations are large plants that generate electricity from nuclear fission in reactors. Most reactors are licensed to run for a set period, and operators can often extend that licence after safety reviews and upgrades. New reactors take many years to plan and build.
why_it_matters: If existing plants keep running longer, countries may be able to meet rising electricity demand without waiting for new nuclear builds, which the headline says are facing delays and rising costs.
open_questions: The sources do not say which governments or plants are involved.
The sources do not give details on the delays or cost rises for new builds.

headline: Google bets on superhot geothermal to power Oregon data centers

facts.text: Houston-based geothermal startup Quaise Energy announced that Google agreed to buy 50 megawatts of carbon-free power from its first commercial project, Project Obsidian, near the Newberry Volcano in central Oregon.
Google said it plans to use the energy to help run its existing data center operations in northwest Oregon as early as 2030.
Quaise confirmed the deal is valued at more than $500 million.
Quaise is working to find offtakers for an additional 200 MW of future capacity at the Oregon site.
Quaise says its Oregon project will cost about $350 million to build.

Quaise plans to initially use oil-and-gas drilling technologies at Project Obsidian to develop an enhanced geothermal system, then switch to millimeter-wave drilling to reach superhot rock above 572 degrees Fahrenheit.
Quaise's millimeter-wave drilling technology has yet to be deployed at commercial scale, and the company is still testing it; it drilled over 330 feet of granite at a Texas field site last year.

Quaise is one of at least four U.S. geothermal companies to sign agreements with tech giants, alongside Fervo Energy's nearly 400 MW deal with Google and Sage Geosystems and XGS Energy partnering with Meta.
Lucia Tian, who leads Google's advanced energy technologies team, told the Wall Street Journal that the scale of power Google needs requires it to foster the broader ecosystem.

context: Geothermal power generates electricity from the Earth's heat, usually by pumping water through hot underground rock to drive turbines. Conventional plants tap relatively shallow resources, while next-generation or enhanced geothermal systems fracture rock to create artificial reservoirs and aim to reach hotter depths. Data centers need steady, around-the-clock clean power, which is why tech companies are signing these deals.
why_it_matters: The deal gives an early-stage superhot geothermal startup a major customer, which the sources say is an essential step toward raising financing for first-of-a-kind facilities. It signals tech companies' demand for clean, continuous power for data centers, including Google's Oregon operations.
open_questions: The sources say the new superhot technology has yet to be deployed widely at commercial scale.
Questions remain about how effectively these geothermal plants can operate over long periods of time.
Quaise still needs offtakers for the additional 200 MW of capacity at the Oregon site.

headline: IAEA working on ceasefire to repair Zaporizhzhia power link

facts.text: The UN nuclear watchdog said it was working with Russia and Ukraine to arrange a new local ceasefire at the Zaporizhzhia plant.
The ceasefire effort follows another loss of offsite power at the plant.
Russian forces seized the Zaporizhzhia plant, Europe's largest with six reactors, in the first weeks of Moscow's February 2022 invasion.
The IAEA said both external power lines were down for the 28th time since the start of the conflict.
Power at the plant was being supplied by diesel generators during the outage.
The IAEA said the power outage was reportedly due to military activity.
The plant's Russian operators said the disconnection occurred after protection devices switched on, and that the diesel generators were working properly.
IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi said the plant's location on the front line results in an extremely precarious offsite power connection.
Grossi called on both sides to work constructively with the IAEA to cease military activity and proceed with repairs.

context: The Zaporizhzhia nuclear power plant in southeastern Ukraine is Europe's largest nuclear plant, with six reactors. The International Atomic Energy Agency is the UN nuclear watchdog that monitors nuclear safety. Nuclear reactors need electricity from external power lines to keep their fuel cool, even when shut down, and backup diesel generators are used when those lines fail.
why_it_matters: Repeated loss of offsite power raises the risk of overheating nuclear fuel at a plant located on an active front line, affecting nuclear safety in the region. The IAEA is seeking a local ceasefire so repairs can proceed.
open_questions: Whether a new local ceasefire will be arranged between Russia and Ukraine.
When the external power lines will be repaired and restored.
Which side's military activity caused the outage, since each side accuses the other.
